WORKSHEET · CLASS 33 · AGES 4–5

Doctor Worksheet for Ages 4–5

A community-helpers worksheet for ages 4–5: trace the word DOCTOR, match the doctor to the stethoscope, bandage and thermometer, circle the healthy habits, count the medicine bottles and draw one way you take care of your body — on screen or on paper.

THE WORKSHEET

The full sheet, exactly as the artist drew it.

See the whole sheet, download the original file or print it from your browser. Want your child to solve it on screen first? The interactive version lives at preschool/4-years/community-helpers-and-our-neighborhood/worksheets/doctor/ / — same sheet, drawing layer included.

HOW TO USE IT

The five steps on the sheet.

  1. 1

    Trace

    Trace the big dotted word DOCTOR letter by letter — say each letter’s name out loud as you go.

  2. 2

    Match

    Draw a line from the doctor to each of his three tools: the stethoscope, the bandage and the thermometer.

  3. 3

    Circle

    Six pictures sit in the grid — circle every one that shows a healthy habit. Look closely: not all six are healthy!

  4. 4

    Count

    Count the orange medicine bottles, then write the number in the box below them.

  5. 5

    Draw

    In the big empty box, draw one thing YOU do to take care of your body — brushing teeth, running, sleeping, anything true.

Before you start, have the words ready: Your child needs a little vocabulary first: a doctor helps sick and hurt people, a stethoscope listens to heartbeats, a bandage protects a healing cut, and a thermometer checks temperature. Say each tool’s name before the pencil starts.

WHY IT HELPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What a doctor’s tools are for, which everyday habits keep bodies healthy, and how to read and write the word DOCTOR.

Doctors become familiar instead of frightening when children meet their tools on paper first. The healthy-habit grid also turns the worksheet into a gentle health talk, and the tracing row builds the same pre-writing muscles the alphabet class uses.

  • Community helper vocabulary
  • Tool matching
  • Healthy-habit awareness
  • Counting to 5
  • Word tracing
  • Drawing from life
FOR GROWN-UPS

Tips, questions and practice.

Say before you start: "This is a doctor — his tools help him take care of people. Trace his name, then find the three tools that belong with him. Now look at the six pictures: which ones show something healthy? Count the bottles slowly with your finger, and finish by drawing how YOU keep your body strong."

Questions to ask: "Which doctor’s tool listens to your heart?" "Why do we wash hands before seeing the doctor?" "Which of the six habits do you do every day?" "What number did the medicine bottles count up to?"

Parent tips: Keep doctor talk friendly and honest — doctors help, and saying how you feel to a doctor is always allowed. Let your child own the pencil: the tracing can be wobbly and the drawing messy; the thinking is the work.

Home practice: Walk the healthy-habit grid at home today: the apple at snack time, the teeth brushing tonight, the running in the yard. Real repetition is what turns a circled picture into a habit.

WORKSHEET · CLASS 33 · AGES 4–5

Firefighter Worksheet for Ages 4–5

A firefighter worksheet for ages 4–5: trace the words FIRE FIGHTER, match the firefighter to the hose, helmet and fire truck, circle the real firefighting tools, count the helmets and draw a safe way to stop, drop and roll — on screen or on paper.

THE WORKSHEET

The full sheet, exactly as the artist drew it.

See the whole sheet, download the original file or print it from your browser. Want your child to solve it on screen first? The interactive version lives at preschool/4-years/community-helpers-and-our-neighborhood/worksheets/firefighter/ / — same sheet, drawing layer included.

HOW TO USE IT

The five steps on the sheet.

  1. 1

    Trace

    Trace the dotted words FIRE FIGHTER across the big row — two words, take them one letter at a time.

  2. 2

    Match

    Draw a line from the firefighter to each piece of his gear: the hose, the helmet and the fire truck.

  3. 3

    Circle

    Six tools sit in the grid — circle every one a firefighter really uses on the job. Two of them belong to other jobs!

  4. 4

    Count

    Count the red fire helmets, then write the number in the box.

  5. 5

    Draw

    Draw a safe way to stop, drop, and roll in the big box — show the rolling!

Before you start, have the words ready: Before starting, name the gear together: the helmet protects the head, the hose carries water, the truck rushes everything to the fire. Explain stop-drop-and-roll in one sentence — if clothes ever catch fire, we stop, drop to the ground, and roll until the fire is out.

WHY IT HELPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What a firefighter wears and carries, which tools fight fires, and the emergency move every child should own: stop, drop and roll.

Fire safety is a skill with real stakes, and rehearsal is what makes it stick. The tool grid sharpens "who uses what" thinking, the helmet count is gentle number practice, and the draw box lets your child rehearse the emergency move with their own hands.

  • Emergency vocabulary
  • Tool matching
  • Stop-drop-and-roll rehearsal
  • Counting to 7
  • Word tracing
  • Safety drawing
FOR GROWN-UPS

Tips, questions and practice.

Say before you start: "This is a firefighter. Trace the two words, then connect him to his hose, his helmet and his truck. Now look at the six tools — a firefighter carries some of them, but a couple belong to a mechanic or a student. Count the helmets with your finger, and then draw the safety move: stop, drop, and roll."

Questions to ask: "What does the hose carry?" "Why does a firefighter wear a helmet?" "Which two tools in the grid are NOT for fighting fires?" "Show me stop, drop, and roll — can you do it on the carpet?"

Parent tips: Practise stop-drop-and-roll for real on a carpet after the sheet — the body remembers what the pencil rehearses. Never make fire scary-for-fun: firefighters are helpers, and practicing the move is what keeps children safe.

Home practice: Visit the drawing at bedtime: ask your child to SHOW the whole family how to stop, drop, and roll. Where is your family’s smoke alarm? Let your child find it — real maps of real safety.

WORKSHEET · CLASS 33 · AGES 4–5

Police Officer Worksheet for Ages 4–5

A police-officer worksheet for ages 4–5: trace the words POLICE OFFICER, match the officer to the badge, radio and patrol car, circle the safety things, count the traffic cones and draw a safe place to cross the street — on screen or on paper.

THE WORKSHEET

The full sheet, exactly as the artist drew it.

See the whole sheet, download the original file or print it from your browser. Want your child to solve it on screen first? The interactive version lives at preschool/4-years/community-helpers-and-our-neighborhood/worksheets/police-officer/ / — same sheet, drawing layer included.

HOW TO USE IT

The five steps on the sheet.

  1. 1

    Trace

    Trace the dotted words POLICE OFFICER — long words, steady lines.

  2. 2

    Match

    Draw a line from the officer to the badge, the radio and the patrol car.

  3. 3

    Circle

    Six things sit in the grid — circle every one that helps keep people safe. One of them is a cuddly friend, not a safety tool!

  4. 4

    Count

    Count the orange traffic cones, then write the number in the box.

  5. 5

    Draw

    Draw a safe place to cross the street — think crosswalk stripes, a crossing guard, held hands.

Before you start, have the words ready: Officers are neighborhood helpers we can trust: the badge shows who they are, the radio calls for help, the patrol car takes them quickly to where they are needed. In any real worry, the plan is the same — find a grown-up you know, and officers are helpers too.

WHY IT HELPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What a police officer carries and drives, which objects help keep people safe, and what a safe street crossing looks like.

Safety tools become recognizable when children sort them on paper. The crossing draw-prompt opens the family conversation about how WE cross — a conversation worth having a hundred times before it is ever needed.

  • Community helper vocabulary
  • Tool matching
  • Safety-object awareness
  • Counting to 5
  • Word tracing
  • Road-safety drawing
FOR GROWN-UPS

Tips, questions and practice.

Say before you start: "This is a police officer — a helper for the whole neighborhood. Trace the words, then connect the badge, the radio and the patrol car. Look at the six pictures: which ones help keep people safe? Count the cones carefully, then draw how WE cross the street safely."

Questions to ask: "What does the badge tell us?" "Which grid pictures keep people safe, and how?" "Who holds your hand when we cross?" "What do the cones tell cars to do?"

Parent tips: Keep the message balanced — officers are helpers AND the first job in any worry is finding a grown-up you know. Practise the real crossing this week with the sheet’s words: stop, look, listen, hold hands.

Home practice: On the next walk, find one real safety thing from the grid — a cone, a helmet rider, a crossing — and name it on the spot. Real streets make the worksheet real.

WORKSHEET · CLASS 33 · AGES 4–5

Nurse Worksheet for Ages 4–5

A nurse worksheet for ages 4–5: trace the word NURSE, match the nurse to the clipboard, bandage and thermometer, circle the healthy habits, count the bandages and draw a way nurses help — on screen or on paper.

THE WORKSHEET

The full sheet, exactly as the artist drew it.

See the whole sheet, download the original file or print it from your browser. Want your child to solve it on screen first? The interactive version lives at preschool/4-years/community-helpers-and-our-neighborhood/worksheets/nurse/ / — same sheet, drawing layer included.

HOW TO USE IT

The five steps on the sheet.

  1. 1

    Trace

    Trace the dotted word NURSE letter by letter — five letters, say each one.

  2. 2

    Match

    Draw a line from the nurse to her clipboard, her bandage and her thermometer.

  3. 3

    Circle

    Five pictures show moments of the day — circle every healthy habit. One of them is a sometimes-treat!

  4. 4

    Count

    Count the bandages in both rows, then write the number in the box.

  5. 5

    Draw

    Draw one way a nurse helps people — wrapping a bandage, checking temperature, a kind smile.

Before you start, have the words ready: Nurses take care of people beside doctors: the clipboard keeps notes, the bandage protects a scrape, the thermometer checks temperature. Nurses explain every step and have gentle hands — a friendly face at any check-up.

WHY IT HELPS

What this worksheet teaches.

Who nurses are and what they carry, which daily habits keep bodies healthy, and caring-in-action — the worksheet’s last box asks your child to draw a nurse’s kindness.

Meeting the nurse on paper makes real check-ups calmer, and the healthy-habit grid doubles as the family’s daily-health talk. The big bandage count is honest two-row counting practice with a purpose.

  • Community helper vocabulary
  • Tool matching
  • Healthy habits
  • Counting to 10
  • Word tracing
  • Empathy drawing
FOR GROWN-UPS

Tips, questions and practice.

Say before you start: "This is a nurse — she takes care of people with gentle hands. Trace her name, then connect her to the clipboard, the bandage and the thermometer. Now the five pictures: which are healthy habits? Count every bandage slowly — there are two rows — and draw how a nurse helps."

Questions to ask: "What does the thermometer check?" "Which habits did you circle, and when did you last do one?" "How many bandages in the top row? And the bottom?" "What would you want a nurse to say to you?"

Parent tips: If a real check-up is coming, this sheet is the warm-up: the nurse will explain first, and telling her how you feel is always allowed. Praise gentle hands during the drawing — kindness is the lesson under the lesson.

Home practice: Play nurse with a teddy tonight: wrap a toilet-paper bandage, check temperature with a hand on the forehead, explain every step out loud — exactly the worksheet, warm and alive.

WORKSHEET · CLASS 33 · AGES 4–5

Teacher Worksheet for Ages 4–5

A teacher worksheet for ages 4–5: trace the word TEACHER, match the teacher to the book, pencil and chalkboard, circle the learning tools, count the pencils and draw your favorite thing to learn — on screen or on paper.

THE WORKSHEET

The full sheet, exactly as the artist drew it.

See the whole sheet, download the original file or print it from your browser. Want your child to solve it on screen first? The interactive version lives at preschool/4-years/community-helpers-and-our-neighborhood/worksheets/teacher/ / — same sheet, drawing layer included.

HOW TO USE IT

The five steps on the sheet.

  1. 1

    Trace

    Trace the dotted word TEACHER across the row — seven letters, nice and steady.

  2. 2

    Match

    Draw a line from the teacher to the book, the pencil and the board.

  3. 3

    Circle

    Five things sit in the row — circle every one we use for learning. One of them belongs on the playground!

  4. 4

    Count

    Count the yellow pencils, then write the number in the box.

  5. 5

    Draw

    Draw your favorite thing to learn in the big box — letters, numbers, dinosaurs, anything!

Before you start, have the words ready: Teachers help children learn letters, numbers, stories and how to be good friends. The board shows the lesson, the book holds the story, the pencil writes the practice. Your child already knows this world — the sheet names it.

WHY IT HELPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What a teacher’s day is full of — books, pencils, a board and questions — plus which objects help learning happen and how to write the word TEACHER.

A child who can name the teacher’s tools walks into any classroom feeling at home. The favorite-thing draw box turns the sheet into a small show-and-tell, and the pencil count is real counting with a real object.

  • School vocabulary
  • Tool matching
  • Learning-object awareness
  • Counting to 4
  • Word tracing
  • Self-expression drawing
FOR GROWN-UPS

Tips, questions and practice.

Say before you start: "This is a teacher — she helps children learn new things every day. Trace her name, then connect the book, the pencil and the board. Look at the five pictures: which help us learn? Count the pencils with your finger, and then draw the thing YOU love learning most."

Questions to ask: "What does the teacher write on the board?" "Which pictures help us learn — and what does each one do?" "How many pencils?" "What is YOUR favorite thing to learn, and who teaches it to you?"

Parent tips: Ask your child to teach the sheet back to you — playing teacher with the worksheet is the deepest rehearsal there is. Name real teachers your child knows and what each one is teaching them this year.

Home practice: Tonight, your child plays teacher with teddies as the class: board, book, pencil — the whole lesson. Ten minutes of teaching-back beats an hour of being taught.

WORKSHEET · CLASS 33 · AGES 4–5

Librarian Worksheet for Ages 4–5

A community-helpers worksheet for ages 4–5: trace the word LIBRARIAN, match the librarian to the books, library card and bookshelf, circle the things that live in a library, count the books and draw your favorite book — on screen or on paper.

THE WORKSHEET

The full sheet, exactly as the artist drew it.

See the whole sheet, download the original file or print it from your browser. Want your child to solve it on screen first? The interactive version lives at preschool/4-years/community-helpers-and-our-neighborhood/worksheets/librarian/ / — same sheet, drawing layer included.

HOW TO USE IT

The five steps on the sheet.

  1. 1

    Trace

    Trace the dotted word LIBRARIAN letter by letter — nine letters, take them one at a time.

  2. 2

    Match

    Draw a line from the librarian to the books, the library card and the bookshelf.

  3. 3

    Circle

    Six pictures sit in the grid — circle every one you could really find in a library. Look closely: would ALL of them be there?

  4. 4

    Count

    Count the books in the count row, then write the number in the box.

  5. 5

    Draw

    Draw your favorite book in the big box — its cover, a character from inside, or the part you love best.

Before you start, have the words ready: A librarian helps people find and borrow books: the library card takes books home for a while, the bookshelf keeps every story tidy, and each book comes back so a friend can enjoy it next. Libraries are quiet, friendly places full of stories.

WHY IT HELPS

What this worksheet teaches.

Who librarians are and what a library holds — books, cards, shelves and computers — plus which everyday objects really belong there and how to write the word LIBRARIAN.

A child who knows how the library works owns it for life. Naming the librarian’s tools turns a first visit from overwhelming to exciting, and the find-it-in-a-library grid builds the careful sorting that later sorts letters, numbers and bugs.

  • Community helper vocabulary
  • Tool matching
  • Place-based sorting
  • Word tracing
  • Counting practice
  • Favorite-book drawing
FOR GROWN-UPS

Tips, questions and practice.

Say before you start: "This is a librarian — she helps people find wonderful books. Trace her name, then connect the books, the library card and the bookshelf. Now look at the six pictures: which ones could you find in a library? Count the books slowly with your finger, and finish by drawing the book YOU love."

Questions to ask: "What does a librarian do all day?" "Which grid pictures could you find at the library?" "What do we do with a book when we finish it?" "What is YOUR favorite book, and who reads it with you?"

Parent tips: Pair the sheet with a real library trip this week — let your child carry the card and hand the books over the desk. Owning the borrowing-and-returning ritual is what quietly makes a reader.

Home practice: Visit the library and play find-it: the bookshelf, the computer, the desk — every circled picture spotted in real life. Then borrow one book and let your child check it out all by themselves.

WORKSHEET · CLASS 33 · AGES 4–5

Farmer Worksheet for Ages 4–5

A community-helpers worksheet for ages 4–5: trace the word FARMER, match the farmer to the tractor, watering can and vegetables, circle the things that grow on a farm, count the carrots and beets and draw a farm scene — on screen or on paper.

THE WORKSHEET

The full sheet, exactly as the artist drew it.

See the whole sheet, download the original file or print it from your browser. Want your child to solve it on screen first? The interactive version lives at preschool/4-years/community-helpers-and-our-neighborhood/worksheets/farmer/ / — same sheet, drawing layer included.

HOW TO USE IT

The five steps on the sheet.

  1. 1

    Trace

    Trace the dotted word FARMER across the row — six letters, nice and steady.

  2. 2

    Match

    Draw a line from the farmer to the tractor, the watering can and the vegetables.

  3. 3

    Circle

    Six pictures sit in the grid — five grow or live on a farm, and one arrived in a delivery box! Circle everything that belongs on the farm.

  4. 4

    Count

    Count the vegetables in the count row — the carrots and the beets — then write the number in the box.

  5. 5

    Draw

    Draw something you might see on a farm in the big box — a barn, an animal, rows of corn, anything farm-fresh.

Before you start, have the words ready: Farmers grow food and care for animals: the tractor pulls and plows, the watering can gives thirsty plants a drink, and vegetables come out of the ground or off the plant. Apples grow on trees, cows give milk, and corn grows tall.

WHY IT HELPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What a farmer grows and raises, which foods start on a farm, and how to tell farm things from store things — plus how to write the word FARMER.

Knowing where food comes from is a superpower for picky eaters — a child who has circled the carrot on a farm sheet meets it on the plate with new interest. The farm grid also plants early thinking about how the world makes things.

  • Farm and food vocabulary
  • Tool matching
  • Where-food-comes-from sorting
  • Word tracing
  • Counting practice
  • Farm-scene drawing
FOR GROWN-UPS

Tips, questions and practice.

Say before you start: "This is a farmer — he grows food and takes care of animals. Trace his name, then connect the tractor, the watering can and the vegetables. Now look at the six pictures: which ones belong on a farm? Count the carrots and beets slowly, and then draw what YOU would see on a farm."

Questions to ask: "What does a tractor do on a farm?" "Which foods in the grid grew on a farm?" "Have you ever pulled a carrot out of the ground?" "What would you feed a cow or a chicken?"

Parent tips: Next grocery trip, play farm-detective: find three foods from the grid and ask who grew each one. If your child is a picky eater, let THEM pick a vegetable from the count row at the store — ownership grows appetites.

Home practice: Try one farm food this week in its simplest form — corn on the cob, a raw carrot with its green top, an apple straight from the bag. Real food, real story, better eating.

WORKSHEET · CLASS 33 · AGES 4–5

Chef Worksheet for Ages 4–5

A community-helpers worksheet for ages 4–5: trace the word CHEF, match the chef to the spoon, mixing bowl and chef hat, circle the healthy foods, count the plates and draw a meal you would like to make — on screen or on paper.

THE WORKSHEET

The full sheet, exactly as the artist drew it.

See the whole sheet, download the original file or print it from your browser. Want your child to solve it on screen first? The interactive version lives at preschool/4-years/community-helpers-and-our-neighborhood/worksheets/chef/ / — same sheet, drawing layer included.

HOW TO USE IT

The five steps on the sheet.

  1. 1

    Trace

    Trace the dotted word CHEF — only four letters, but say each one loud and proud.

  2. 2

    Match

    Draw a line from the chef to the spoon, the mixing bowl and the chef hat.

  3. 3

    Circle

    Six foods sit in the grid — circle every one that helps your body grow strong. Two of them are sometimes-treats!

  4. 4

    Count

    Count the plates, then write the number in the box.

  5. 5

    Draw

    Draw a meal you would like to make in the big box — breakfast, lunch, dinner or a silly sandwich.

Before you start, have the words ready: A chef cooks for other people: the spoon stirs, the mixing bowl holds everything together, and the tall hat is called a toque — real chefs really wear it! Kitchens are busy places where good food and clean hands matter most.

WHY IT HELPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What a chef does in a kitchen, which tools cook a meal, and which foods help bodies grow — plus how to write the short but mighty word CHEF.

Chefs make healthy food look exciting, and this sheet borrows that magic. The healthy-food grid turns into a plate conversation at exactly the age when food habits form, and the meal-drawing box lets your child design a menu of their own.

  • Kitchen vocabulary
  • Tool matching
  • Healthy-food sorting
  • Word tracing
  • Counting practice
  • Meal drawing
FOR GROWN-UPS

Tips, questions and practice.

Say before you start: "This is a chef — he cooks wonderful food for people. Trace his name, then connect the spoon, the mixing bowl and the hat. Now look at the six foods: which ones are healthy helpers for your body? Count the plates carefully, and then draw the meal YOU would love to make."

Questions to ask: "What does the chef stir in the big bowl?" "Which foods did you circle, and why?" "What is a sometimes food in our family?" "What would your restaurant serve first?"

Parent tips: Let tonight’s dinner be the drawn meal for real if you can — even one food from your child’s menu on the plate makes the worksheet delicious. Chefs wash hands first: borrow that rule too.

Home practice: Cook one simple thing together this week — stirring the pancake batter counts. The spoon, the bowl, the tasting: the whole worksheet, warm and edible.

WORKSHEET · CLASS 33 · AGES 4–5

Dentist Worksheet for Ages 4–5

A community-helpers worksheet for ages 4–5: trace the word DENTIST, match the dentist to the toothbrush, mirror and tooth, circle the teeth-healthy habits, count the toothbrushes and draw yourself brushing — on screen or on paper.

THE WORKSHEET

The full sheet, exactly as the artist drew it.

See the whole sheet, download the original file or print it from your browser. Want your child to solve it on screen first? The interactive version lives at preschool/4-years/community-helpers-and-our-neighborhood/worksheets/dentist/ / — same sheet, drawing layer included.

HOW TO USE IT

The five steps on the sheet.

  1. 1

    Trace

    Trace the dotted word DENTIST letter by letter — seven letters, steady as a dental chair.

  2. 2

    Match

    Draw a line from the dentist to the toothbrush, the mirror and the tooth.

  3. 3

    Circle

    Four pictures show moments of the day — circle every habit that keeps teeth happy and healthy. One of them is a sweet trick!

  4. 4

    Count

    Count the toothbrushes, then write the number in the box.

  5. 5

    Draw

    Draw yourself brushing your teeth in the big box — open wide, brush up and down, front and back!

Before you start, have the words ready: The dentist looks after teeth: the toothbrush sweeps away sugar bugs, the little mirror shows the teeth hiding at the back, and every tooth gets a check. Teeth like brushing, water, good food and sleep — sugar makes the sugar bugs dance.

WHY IT HELPS

What this worksheet teaches.

Who the dentist is and what happens in the chair, which daily habits keep teeth strong, and how to write the word DENTIST — a gentle warm-up for real check-ups.

Check-ups go better when the chair is familiar on paper first. The habits grid turns brushing from a nightly battle into a job your child owns, and drawing themselves brushing rehearses the very routine parents ask for twice a day.

  • Community helper vocabulary
  • Tool matching
  • Teeth-healthy habits
  • Word tracing
  • Counting practice
  • Routine drawing
FOR GROWN-UPS

Tips, questions and practice.

Say before you start: "This is a dentist — she keeps your teeth strong and healthy. Trace her name, then connect the toothbrush, the mirror and the tooth. Now look at the four pictures: which things keep teeth happy? Count the toothbrushes, and then draw YOU brushing — big smile, of course."

Questions to ask: "What does the dentist’s mirror do?" "Which habits keep teeth strong?" "What does sugar do to teeth?" "When do YOU brush — and who checks the back teeth?"

Parent tips: Dentists are helpers, and the mirror is their flashlight — say that before a real appointment and the chair feels friendlier. Tonight, brush to a song your child chooses: two minutes, twice a day, exactly what the sheet teaches.

Home practice: Brush together tonight and let your child be the dentist for YOUR teeth for one minute — teaching back is the deepest practice there is. Then let them check their own smile in the mirror, just like the sheet.

WORKSHEET · CLASS 33 · AGES 4–5

Veterinarian Worksheet for Ages 4–5

A community-helpers worksheet for ages 4–5: trace the word VETERINARIAN, match the vet to the cat, stethoscope and paw print, circle what pets need to stay healthy, count the pet bowls and draw an animal to care for — on screen or on paper.

THE WORKSHEET

The full sheet, exactly as the artist drew it.

See the whole sheet, download the original file or print it from your browser. Want your child to solve it on screen first? The interactive version lives at preschool/4-years/community-helpers-and-our-neighborhood/worksheets/veterinarian/ / — same sheet, drawing layer included.

HOW TO USE IT

The five steps on the sheet.

  1. 1

    Trace

    Trace the dotted word VETERINARIAN — a very long word! Take it letter by letter, and say each one.

  2. 2

    Match

    Draw a line from the veterinarian to her patient — the cat — and to the stethoscope and the paw print.

  3. 3

    Circle

    Six pictures sit in the grid — circle every one that helps a pet stay healthy. The green checkmark counts too: it is the vet check-up!

  4. 4

    Count

    Count the pet bowls, then write the number in the box.

  5. 5

    Draw

    Draw an animal you would like to care for in the big box — real or imaginary, as long as it gets love.

Before you start, have the words ready: A veterinarian is an animal doctor: the stethoscope listens to hearts and lungs, the food and water bowls keep pets strong, the brush keeps fur tidy, and the green check is the check-up — the vet’s way of saying all is well. Pets need care every single day.

WHY IT HELPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What a veterinarian does for animals, which things keep pets fed, watered, groomed and checked, and how to write the very long word VETERINARIAN.

Caring for a pet on paper is rehearsal for caring in real life. The needs grid builds empathy — a pet is not a toy but a small life with needs — and the long trace word is a proud badge for children ready to stretch their pencil muscles.

  • Community helper vocabulary
  • Tool matching
  • Pet-needs awareness
  • Word tracing
  • Counting practice
  • Empathy drawing
FOR GROWN-UPS

Tips, questions and practice.

Say before you start: "This is a veterinarian — an animal doctor! Trace the long, long name, then connect her to her cat patient, the stethoscope and the paw print. Now look at the six pictures: which ones help a pet stay healthy? Count the pet bowls, and then draw the animal YOU would love to take care of."

Questions to ask: "What does a veterinarian do?" "What does a pet you know need every single day?" "What happens at a pet check-up?" "How do you know an animal feels happy or scared?"

Parent tips: If a real vet visit is coming, this sheet is the warm-up: the vet will look with a light, listen with a stethoscope and explain first — exactly like the doctor, but for animals. Let your child bring the drawn animal along in their pocket.

Home practice: Care for a real or stuffed animal tonight: fill a water bowl, brush fur with a soft brush, and give a full check-up with a gentle voice — every step explained out loud, exactly like the sheet.

WORKSHEET · CLASS 33 · AGES 4–5

Paramedic Worksheet for Ages 4–5

A community-helpers worksheet for ages 4–5: trace the word PARAMEDIC, match the paramedic to the ambulance, first-aid bag and bandage, circle the helper tools, count the bandages and draw an ambulance — on screen or on paper.

THE WORKSHEET

The full sheet, exactly as the artist drew it.

See the whole sheet, download the original file or print it from your browser. Want your child to solve it on screen first? The interactive version lives at preschool/4-years/community-helpers-and-our-neighborhood/worksheets/paramedic/ / — same sheet, drawing layer included.

HOW TO USE IT

The five steps on the sheet.

  1. 1

    Trace

    Trace the dotted word PARAMEDIC letter by letter — nine letters for a very fast helper.

  2. 2

    Match

    Draw a line from the paramedic to the ambulance, the first-aid bag and the bandage.

  3. 3

    Circle

    Six pictures sit in the grid — circle every one that helps a person who is hurt. Some of them belong in the kitchen or the toy box instead!

  4. 4

    Count

    Count the bandages, then write the number in the box.

  5. 5

    Draw

    Draw an ambulance in the big box — lights on top, wheels below, and a big friendly cross.

Before you start, have the words ready: A paramedic is a medical helper who comes fast when someone is hurt: the ambulance carries them and their equipment, the first-aid bag holds the tools, and a bandage protects a scrape while it heals. Paramedics check, calm, and take people to more help.

WHY IT HELPS

What this worksheet teaches.

Who paramedics are and how they rush to help, which tools treat a hurt person, and the big idea that calling for help is brave and smart — plus how to write the word PARAMEDIC.

Meeting the ambulance on paper turns the loudest siren into a friendly sound that means HELP IS COMING. The tools grid sorts real helper tools from household look-alikes, and the safety talk that comes with this sheet is one families never regret.

  • Emergency helper vocabulary
  • Tool matching
  • Helper-tool sorting
  • Word tracing
  • Counting practice
  • Ambulance drawing
FOR GROWN-UPS

Tips, questions and practice.

Say before you start: "This is a paramedic — a helper who rushes to people who are hurt. Trace the name, then connect the ambulance, the first-aid bag and the bandage. Now the six pictures: which ones help an injured person? Count the bandages slowly, and then draw an ambulance with its lights shining."

Questions to ask: "What does the siren tell other cars?" "Which tools in the grid help someone who is hurt?" "What number do we call when we need help?" "Who are OUR grown-ups to run to in any emergency?"

Parent tips: Teach your child your local emergency number and their grown-ups’ real names — not just Mom and Dad — and rehearse it like a song. Paramedics are helpers, and knowing the plan makes children calm and brave, never scared.

Home practice: Pack a small family first-aid kit together and let your child place each thing in: bandages, wipes, a thermometer. Name every item like the sheet does — then rehearse the emergency plan once, calm and proud.

WORKSHEET · CLASS 33 · AGES 4–5

Crossing Guard Worksheet for Ages 4–5

A community-helpers worksheet for ages 4–5: trace the words CROSSING GUARD, match the guard to the stop sign, vest and crosswalk, circle the safe crossing rules, count the stop signs and draw yourself crossing safely — on screen or on paper.

THE WORKSHEET

The full sheet, exactly as the artist drew it.

See the whole sheet, download the original file or print it from your browser. Want your child to solve it on screen first? The interactive version lives at preschool/4-years/community-helpers-and-our-neighborhood/worksheets/crossing-guard/ / — same sheet, drawing layer included.

HOW TO USE IT

The five steps on the sheet.

  1. 1

    Trace

    Trace the dotted words CROSSING GUARD — two words, one letter at a time.

  2. 2

    Match

    Draw a line from the crossing guard to the stop sign, the vest and the crosswalk.

  3. 3

    Circle

    Four rules sit in the grid, each written in words — circle every SAFE way to cross the street. One of the four is a big mistake!

  4. 4

    Count

    Count the stop signs, then write the number in the box.

  5. 5

    Draw

    Draw yourself crossing safely in the big box — crosswalk stripes, looking eyes, and a grown-up’s hand.

Before you start, have the words ready: A crossing guard stops traffic so children can cross: the stop sign tells cars to wait, the bright vest makes the guard easy to see, and the crosswalk is the one place feet belong on the road. The rules: look left, right, then left again; raise your hand and wait; use the crosswalk — never run across.

WHY IT HELPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What a crossing guard does at the corner, the four rules of a safe street crossing, and which rules are safe and which are not — plus how to write the words CROSSING GUARD.

Street crossing is the highest-stakes skill on the whole neighborhood walk, and rehearsal is what makes it stick. Sorting safe from unsafe rules lets your child explain the WHY back to you — a far stronger memory than a rule recited once.

  • Community helper vocabulary
  • Tool matching
  • Street-safety rules
  • Safe-versus-unsafe sorting
  • Word tracing
  • Safety drawing
FOR GROWN-UPS

Tips, questions and practice.

Say before you start: "This is a crossing guard — the helper who keeps the corner safe. Trace the two words, then connect the stop sign, the vest and the crosswalk. Now read the four rules together: which ones are safe? Count the stop signs, and then draw YOU crossing — stripes, eyes left and right, hand in hand."

Questions to ask: "What does the stop sign tell the cars?" "Which three rules are safe?" "Why do we look left, right, then left again?" "Who holds your hand at the crossing — and when may you cross alone?"

Parent tips: Walk to a real crossing this week and act out all four rules — look left, right, then left again, hand raised at the curb, crosswalk only, walking feet. Practised feet are safe feet, and the guard’s wave is a friend’s wave.

Home practice: On every walk this week, let your child be the crossing captain: stop at the curb, look left-right-left, hold hands, walk. Ten real crossings beat ten worksheets — and you will both know the rules by heart.

WORKSHEET · CLASS 33 · AGES 4–5

Bus Driver Worksheet for Ages 4–5

A community-helpers worksheet for ages 4–5: trace the words BUS DRIVER, match the driver to the school bus, steering wheel and stop sign, circle the safe bus rules, count the windows and draw a safe bus stop — on screen or on paper.

THE WORKSHEET

The full sheet, exactly as the artist drew it.

See the whole sheet, download the original file or print it from your browser. Want your child to solve it on screen first? The interactive version lives at preschool/4-years/community-helpers-and-our-neighborhood/worksheets/bus-driver/ / — same sheet, drawing layer included.

HOW TO USE IT

The five steps on the sheet.

  1. 1

    Trace

    Trace the dotted words BUS DRIVER — two words, steady lines, just like the driver’s hands on the wheel.

  2. 2

    Match

    Draw a line from the bus driver to the school bus, the steering wheel and the stop sign.

  3. 3

    Circle

    Four rules sit in the grid, each written in words — circle every SAFE way to ride the bus. One of the four is wobbly and wrong!

  4. 4

    Count

    Count the windows on the little bus, then write the number in the box.

  5. 5

    Draw

    Draw a safe school-bus stop in the big box — you waiting back from the curb, the bus coming, your grown-up nearby.

Before you start, have the words ready: The bus driver steers a big, heavy vehicle full of children and must watch the road, not the noise. The rules: stay seated while the bus moves, keep hands and feet to yourself, use a quiet voice — and never run in the aisle. The stop sign on the bus tells cars to wait for children.

WHY IT HELPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What a bus driver does, the four rules of riding the school bus safely, and which rules are safe and which are not — plus how to write the words BUS DRIVER.

The school bus is often a child’s first ride without a parent, and knowing the rules turns nerves into pride. Safe-versus-unsafe sorting lets your child rehearse the aisle, the seat and the stop before the first real ride — the best kind of readiness.

  • Community helper vocabulary
  • Tool matching
  • Bus-safety rules
  • Safe-versus-unsafe sorting
  • Word tracing
  • Bus-stop drawing
FOR GROWN-UPS

Tips, questions and practice.

Say before you start: "This is the bus driver — she drives the school bus and keeps every rider safe. Trace the two words, then connect the school bus, the steering wheel and the stop sign. Now the four rules: which are safe? Count the little bus’s windows, and then draw your own safe bus stop."

Questions to ask: "What does the bus’s stop sign tell the cars?" "Which three bus rules are safe?" "Why do we stay seated while the bus moves?" "Where do we stand while we wait for the bus?"

Parent tips: Wait for the bus back from the curb, and wait for the driver’s signal before crossing in front — teach those two moves this week and your child owns the whole ride. Drivers are helpers; a wave and a good-morning is friendly practice.

Home practice: Next time you ride any bus or car, rehearse the rules in miniature: bottoms on seats, quiet voices, hands to yourself. The big yellow bus will feel like a friend when the day comes.

WORKSHEET · CLASS 33 · AGES 4–5

Mail Carrier Worksheet for Ages 4–5

A community-helpers worksheet for ages 4–5: trace the words MAIL CARRIER, match the carrier to the envelope, stamp and mailbox, circle what travels in the mail, count the letters and draw a letter to send — on screen or on paper.

THE WORKSHEET

The full sheet, exactly as the artist drew it.

See the whole sheet, download the original file or print it from your browser. Want your child to solve it on screen first? The interactive version lives at preschool/4-years/community-helpers-and-our-neighborhood/worksheets/mail-carrier/ / — same sheet, drawing layer included.

HOW TO USE IT

The five steps on the sheet.

  1. 1

    Trace

    Trace the dotted words MAIL CARRIER — two words for the person who walks the whole neighborhood.

  2. 2

    Match

    Draw a line from the mail carrier to the envelope, the stamp and the mailbox.

  3. 3

    Circle

    Six pictures sit in the grid — circle every one that truly belongs in the mail. Some are sure friends of the mailbox; some are sneaky visitors!

  4. 4

    Count

    Count the letters in the pile, then write the number in the box.

  5. 5

    Draw

    Draw a letter you would like to send in the big box — to a grandparent, a friend, or a faraway cousin.

Before you start, have the words ready: A mail carrier brings letters and packages to every door: the envelope holds the words, the stamp is the ticket that pays for the trip, and the mailbox is where the journey starts and ends. Flat things ride in envelopes; bigger things ride in boxes.

WHY IT HELPS

What this worksheet teaches.

How a letter travels from a hand to a mailbox across town, what the mail carrier carries, and which things really travel through the mail — plus how to write the words MAIL CARRIER.

Sending real mail is a disappearing joy, and this sheet hands it back. Naming the mail’s journey builds the idea that messages travel — the seed of understanding addresses, maps and how people stay in touch across any distance.

  • Community helper vocabulary
  • Tool matching
  • Mail sorting
  • Word tracing
  • Counting practice
  • Letter drawing
FOR GROWN-UPS

Tips, questions and practice.

Say before you start: "This is a mail carrier — the helper who brings letters to every door. Trace the two words, then connect the envelope, the stamp and the mailbox. Now the six pictures: which ones travel through the mail? Count the letters in the pile, and then draw a letter YOU would like to send."

Questions to ask: "What does the stamp do?" "Where does a letter start its journey and where does it end?" "Which grid things would you post, and which would you keep?" "Who would YOU send a letter to first?"

Parent tips: Make the sheet real: help your child draw the letter from the last box, fold it into an envelope, add a stamp and post it today. A real reply, days later, is the most magical follow-up lesson there is.

Home practice: Write and post one real letter this week — a thank-you, a drawing, three words to grandma. Then walk past your own mailbox together and wait. Real mail beats any worksheet every single time.

Baker Worksheet for Ages 4–5

A community-helpers worksheet for ages 4–5: trace the word BAKER, match the baker to the bread, mixing bowl and oven mitt, circle the bakes, count the cupcakes and draw a treat you would like to bake — on screen or on paper.

THE WORKSHEET

The full sheet, exactly as the artist drew it.

See the whole sheet, download the original file or print it from your browser. Want your child to solve it on screen first? The interactive version lives at preschool/4-years/community-helpers-and-our-neighborhood/worksheets/baker/ / — same sheet, drawing layer included.

HOW TO USE IT

The five steps on the sheet.

  1. 1

    Trace

    Trace the dotted word BAKER across the row — five letters, warm as fresh bread.

  2. 2

    Match

    Draw a line from the baker to the bread, the mixing bowl and the oven mitt.

  3. 3

    Circle

    Six foods sit in the grid — circle every one a baker can bake in the oven. Five come out golden; one grows on a tree!

    Draw

WHY IT HELPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What a baker makes before the town wakes up, which tools bake bread and cakes, and which foods come from an oven — plus how to write the word BAKER.

Bakers turn simple flour into celebration food, and children know it in their bones. The baked-versus-grown sorting builds category thinking, and the treat-draw box opens the lovely family talk about which treats are worth baking together.

  • Kitchen vocabulary
  • Tool matching
  • Baked-versus-grown sorting
  • Word tracing
  • Counting practice
  • Treat drawing
FOR GROWN-UPS

Tips, questions and practice.

Say before you start: "This is a baker — she makes bread and treats while the town is still asleep. Trace her name, then connect the bread, the mixing bowl and the oven mitt. Now the six foods: which ones does the oven make? Count the cupcakes slowly, and then draw the treat YOU would bake."

Questions to ask: "What does the baker pull out of the oven?" "Which foods in the grid did somebody bake?" "Why does the baker wear the big mitt?" "What would you bake first — and who would you share it with?"

Parent tips: Baking together is measuring, counting and patience in one delicious lesson — one batch of anything this week is enough. Let your child own the mixing and the pouring; the flour mess is the tuition.

Home practice: Bake one simple treat together this week — even a ready-mix counts. Let your child wear the mitt for real (empty-handed first!) and pull the tray out with you. The worksheet, but edible.

Tips, questions and practice.

Say before you start: "This is a delivery driver — the helper who brings things right to our door. Trace the two words, then connect the van, the package and the address label. Now the six pictures: every one of them can ride in the van! Circle them all. Count the packages, and then draw a package YOU would send — who is it for?"

Questions to ask: "What does the address label do?" "Which grid things have YOU seen a van deliver?" "What happens if the label has the wrong name?" "Who would YOU send a package to, and what would be inside?"

Home practice: Send one real package this month — cookies to a cousin, a drawing to a friend — and let your child help write the address label and drop it off. Watching it arrive is the best worksheet follow-up there is.

Florist Worksheet for Ages 4–5

The five steps on the sheet.

    Trace

    Match

    Draw a line from the florist to the flowers, the vase and the watering can.

    Circle

  5. 5

    Draw

    Draw a colorful bouquet in the big box — every flower a different color, and one for someone you love.

Before you start, have the words ready: A florist works with flowers: the vase holds the bouquet, the watering can gives each stem a drink, and every flower in the shop was once a seed that needed sun, rain and soil. Chocolate cake is wonderful — but no plant ever grew from cake!

WHY IT HELPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What a florist arranges and sells, what every plant needs to grow — sun, water and care — and how to tell plant-helpers from party guests — plus how to write the word FLORIST.

This sheet hides a science lesson inside a flower shop: what a living thing truly needs. The plant-needs grid builds the earliest biology sorting there is, and the bouquet draw box ends the sheet with generosity — flowers are how people say kind things.

  • Plant-needs sorting

  • Counting practice
  • Bouquet drawing
FOR GROWN-UPS

Tips, questions and practice.

Say before you start: "This is a florist — the helper who makes bouquets out of flowers. Trace the name, then connect the flowers, the vase and the watering can. Now the six pictures: which ones help plants grow? Count the flowers petal by petal, and then draw a bouquet — who should we pretend to give it to?"

Questions to ask: "What does a florist sell?" "What three things does every plant need to grow?" "Which grid tiles are party guests instead?" "Who would you give a real bouquet to, and why?"

Parent tips: Grow something this week — a bean in a wet cotton ball counts completely. Let your child water it with a real can and watch for the first sprout: the grid’s sun, water and seedling, alive on a windowsill.

Home practice: Buy or pick three stems this week and let your child arrange, water and display them — then deliver one flower to a neighbor. Flowers are kindness with stems; the sheet just says it in pencil.

The full sheet, exactly as the artist drew it.

See the whole sheet, download the original file or print it from your browser. Want your child to solve it on screen first? The interactive version lives at preschool/4-years/community-helpers-and-our-neighborhood/worksheets/lifeguard/ / — same sheet, drawing layer included.

HOW TO USE IT

The five steps on the sheet.

  1. 1

    Trace

    Trace the dotted word LIFEGUARD letter by letter — nine letters for the watcher of the water.

  2. 2

    Match

    Draw a line from the lifeguard to the whistle, the rescue float and the pool.

  3. 3

    Circle

    Four labeled rules sit in the grid, some with a green check and some with a red cross — circle every SAFE rule. Two are safe and two are not!

    Draw yourself being safe near water in the big box — swimming beside a grown-up, or walking feet on the wet deck.

Before you start, have the words ready: A lifeguard sits high where the whole pool is in view, with a whistle for warnings and a rescue float for saving. The safe rules on this sheet: swim with a grown-up and walk on the pool deck. The tricky two? Running near the pool and diving in the shallow end — the red cross and green check marks have opinions about all four!

WHY IT HELPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What a lifeguard watches for at the pool, the safe swimming rules on the sheet — and the two unsafe ones to catch — plus how to write the word LIFEGUARD.

Water is the most serious safety topic in this whole collection, and four-year-olds are exactly the right age to start the rules. The check-and-cross marks let your child judge each rule out loud — sorting safe from unsafe is the core skill of every pool summer to come.

  • Community helper vocabulary
  • Pool-safety rules

  • Tool matching
  • Word tracing

FOR GROWN-UPS

Tips, questions and practice.

Say before you start: "This is a lifeguard — the helper who watches over everyone in the water. Trace the name, then connect the whistle, the rescue float and the pool. Now the four rules: which are safe? The green checks and red crosses have opinions! Count the beach balls, and then draw YOU being safe near water."

Questions to ask: "What does the lifeguard’s whistle mean?" "Which two rules are safe, and what makes them safe?" "Why do we walk near the pool?" "Who is YOUR grown-up in the water, every single time?"

Parent tips: The non-negotiables, said warmly and often: never swim without a grown-up, walk on the deck, and ask before going near ANY water — pools, buckets, ponds. Practise the walking feet on a real deck edge this summer; legs remember what pencils rehearse.

Home practice: At the next pool or bath, rehearse the sheet: grown-up first, walking feet, ask permission. Give your child the job of spotting the real lifeguard at every pool you visit — the watcher of the water, found in real life.

One is quiet as a nap and one just turns the volume up! Count the instruments, and then draw one YOU would love to play."

Questions to ask: "Which would you strum, tap or shake?" "Why does the book belong to the reader, not the band?" "What does the microphone do to a voice?" "What sound does YOUR dream instrument make?"

Parent tips: Real instrument play beats any grid: a pot-and-wooden-spoon drum kit is a full concert. If music lessons are on the horizon, this sheet is the warm-up — name the instrument, hold the air-guitar, and let the want grow on its own.

Home practice: Have a kitchen-band concert tonight: one pot drummer, one shaker in a bottle, one singer with a pretend microphone — the grid, brought to life at full volume. Curtain call at bedtime.

What this worksheet teaches.

What a park ranger does in the park, four real ways to care for nature, and why trails, water and wild plants deserve gentle hands — plus how to write the words PARK RANGER.

Nature care is citizenship in small shoes: every rule on this grid is one a four-year-old can actually keep. The all-correct grid builds pride instead of worry — your child is the helper nature has been waiting for.

Say before you start: "This is a park ranger — the helper who takes care of the whole park. Trace the two words, then connect the backpack, the map and the trail sign. Now the four pictures: every single one is a way to care for nature! Circle them all. Count the trees, and then draw YOUR trail — where does it lead?"

Questions to ask: "What does the park ranger protect?" "Which caring ways will YOU do on our next walk?" "Why do we stay on the trail?" "What does the map help the ranger find?"

Parent tips: Adopt one ranger rule per walk this month: trash out, feet on the trail, plants left for the bees. A small backpack your child carries — with a pocket for collecting litter — turns the whole sheet into a uniform.

Home practice: Walk a real trail this week as junior rangers: pack the backpack, read the trail sign, stay on the path and carry out one piece of litter each. The park gets cleaner; the habit gets permanent.

Photographer Worksheet for Ages 4–5

A community-helpers worksheet for ages 4–5: trace the word PHOTOGRAPHER, match the photographer to the camera, lens and photo, circle the photographer’s tools, count the cameras and draw a picture to take — on screen or on paper.

The five steps on the sheet.

  1. 1

    Trace

    Trace the dotted word PHOTOGRAPHER letter by letter — a long, long word with twelve letters. Slow and steady, like a tripod.

  2. 2

    Match

    Draw a line from the photographer to the camera, the lens and the photo.

  3. 3

    Circle

  4. 4

    Count

    Draw

    Draw a picture you would like to photograph in the big box — a pet, a person, a place, or a moment that never sits still.

Before you start, have the words ready: A photographer captures moments: the camera takes the picture, the lens decides how close it looks, and the photo is the memory you can keep. Tripods hold the camera still, bags carry the gear, and even a phone can be a camera. Two tiles in the grid belong to other jobs entirely — the artist’s paintbrush and the ball game!

WHY IT HELPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What a photographer does behind the camera, which tools take, steady and store pictures, and which grid tiles sneak in from other jobs — plus how to write the word PHOTOGRAPHER.

Photographers freeze time, and children love that power. The nine-tile grid is the set’s biggest sorting challenge — perfect for a child ready to think job by job — and the photograph-draw box turns the sheet into a shot list for a real walk with a real camera.

Tips, questions and practice.

Say before you start: "This is a photographer — the helper who catches moments and keeps them forever. Trace the long name, then connect the camera, the lens and the photo. Now the big grid of nine: which things help take or keep a picture? Two belong to other jobs! Count the cameras, and then draw the photo YOU would take."

Questions to ask: "What does the tripod hold up?" "Which two grid tiles belong to other jobs — and whose jobs are they?" "Could a phone be a camera too?" "What moment would YOU freeze forever?"

Parent tips: Hand over a real camera — an old phone is perfect — and give the drawn shot list a test walk: one picture of a pet, one of a person, one of something tiny. Ask your child to pick ONE favorite and say why; that is a photographer’s eye, born.

Home practice: On your next walk, let your child be the family photographer with ten pictures of anything. Print or display one photo and let them caption it — a real photo, a real title, a real gallery debut.

    Trace

Here is the sorting secret — a banana peel is not trash to a garden: it composts into food for new plants!

WHY IT HELPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What sanitation workers do for the whole town, which items go in the recycling bin, and where the rest belongs — compost, trash or the bin — plus how to write the words SANITATION WORKER.

This sheet explains the people behind the early-morning rumble — helpers children hear every week but rarely meet. The recycle-or-not grid builds real sorting skills your own kitchen bin can use tonight, and the safety rule is worth its weight: never chase or hide near a working truck.

FOR GROWN-UPS

Tips, questions and practice.

Say before you start: "This is a sanitation worker — the helper who keeps our whole town clean and healthy. Trace the two words, then connect the garbage truck, the recycling bin and the gloves. Now the six items: which ones can be recycled? One is a snack’s coat and one is a snack itself! Count the bins, and then draw how WE keep our streets clean."

Questions to ask: "What does the garbage truck do on our street?" "Which four things go in the recycling bin?" "Where does the banana peel go instead — and what does it become?" "What do the safety gloves do?"

Parent tips: Trucks and bins are work zones: keep little watchers well back on collection day — never behind a reversing truck, never inside a bin. Then sort tonight’s recycling together and let your child be the checker: bottle, box, can, jar — the sheet, done for real.

Home practice: Start a small compost jar or corner this week for peels and apple cores — let your child feed it daily and watch it change. The grid’s trickiest tile becomes a living science experiment on the windowsill.
